nameStory: Kurtziella cerina gets its scientific name from the genus Kurtziella, named after a malacologist (shell scientist), while 'cerina' comes from the Latin word meaning 'waxy' or 'wax-colored.' This likely refers to the shell's pale, waxy appearance when found on the beach.
description: Kurtziella cerina is a tiny predatory sea snail that hunts other small marine creatures along New England's coast. These miniature mollusks have elongated, spiral shells that are quite small - you'd need to look closely to spot one on the beach. Like other sea snails, they carry their coiled home on their back and can retreat inside when threatened. They're part of a group called marine gastropods, which simply means 'stomach-foot' - referring to how they glide along on their muscular underside.

idTips.label: Shell shape
idTips.description: Look for a small, elongated spiral shell that's taller than it is wide, tapering to a pointed spire at the top

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small - often less than half an inch long, requiring close examination to identify properly

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Shell has a waxy, pale appearance ranging from cream to light brown, sometimes with a subtle sheen

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Shell surface feels smooth to slightly rough when touched, with fine spiral ridges visible under close inspection

idTips.label: Habitat clue
idTips.description: Found in marine environments, often buried in sand or mud, or crawling on seaweed and rocks

habitat: This tiny snail lives in shallow coastal waters throughout New England, from sandy bottoms to rocky intertidal zones. You're most likely to find empty shells washed up on beaches after storms, or spot living specimens in tide pools among seaweed and under rocks. They prefer areas with some shelter and food sources like other small invertebrates.

seasonality.spring: Active as waters warm up, but difficult to spot due to small size. Look for tiny shells in beach wrack after spring storms.
seasonality.summer: Most active period when they're hunting and reproducing. Best time to find living specimens in tide pools during low tide.
seasonality.fall: Still active in early fall, but storm activity may wash more empty shells onto beaches for easier discovery.
seasonality.winter: Less active in cold water. Empty shells from winter storms may accumulate in beach drift lines.

funFact: Despite being smaller than your pinky nail, this tiny snail is a fierce predator that uses a specialized feeding structure called a radula - like a microscopic chainsaw made of teeth - to drill into other small creatures and slurp out their insides!
confusionNotes: With only 34 recorded observations in New England, this species is easily confused with other tiny marine snails found on beaches. The key is the elongated, waxy-looking shell - many similar species are rounder or have different surface textures.
contextualKnowledge: The family name Mangeliidae might sound intimidating, but it's just the scientific grouping for these small predatory sea snails. Don't let the technical terms discourage you - these are simply tiny marine hunters that play important roles in coastal ecosystems.
compareHints: Since Kurtziella cerina appears to be the only species in its genus recorded in New England waters, compare it with other small Mangeliidae family members by focusing on the elongated shell shape and waxy coloration. Other small predatory snails in the region tend to be either more rounded or have distinctly different surface patterns and colors.
